surfaces.part: side piers and gate panel with water

answer.evidence: A crossbeam spans the full width at rows 6-10. It has a light back highlight at row 6, a mid-tone band at rows 7-8, and a light front-edge line at row 9. Darker rows 10-11 follow as eave shadow, so the beam reads as a thin top surface of about 4 rows. Below it, rows 11-31 are the front face: stone piers on both sides and a central channel with gate bars, a pale water lip at rows 22-23 and water below. The strip at rows 1-3 with the red wheel is a front-facing beam with no edge line. This is a borderline case because the top band is thin and could also be read as a front-facing striped lintel.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a stone sluice gate with a red wheel on top and flowing water. It holds up against the references on the measured facts. It has 21 distinct colours per 16x16 tile, against 20 for the roofed well and 17 for the cheese stall. It has 0% 5x5 flat-fill coverage and 29 distinct colours overall. Only 3% of its dark edge pixels are neutral, so the outline carries a tint (dark blue-grey and dark stone tones) rather than a black sticker line, much like the tinted outlines on the hedge and stall. By eye, the stone blocks show about five lightness steps with per-block variation, and the water has several blues with highlight streaks. This is slightly less layered than the well's roof and stonework, but it is not shallow. A careful artist would accept it next to the references without it looking flatter or more sticker-like. The picture is small and low in resolution, so I rely partly on the measured facts.

answer.evidence: Rows 6-9 form a light horizontal band across the full 32px width. Below it, rows 11-31 are a tall front face: stone pillars, a dark gate frame with slats, and water. Rows 1-3 are a front-facing beam strip with the red wheel and are not counted as a top. The top is thin (about 4 rows) but has an edge line and shadow, so the reading is only marginally three_quarter.
